senses: The role or responsibilities of a pastor.
The period of service of a particular pastor to their congregation; their term of office.
An organization or body consisting of multiple pastors.
ety: From pastor + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office, a body of people involved with it).
examples: The old pastor found his pastorate wearying, and longed to retire.
His pastorate had been marked by several changes in church policy with regards to community outreach.
At the denomination's annual conference, the pastorate had passed a bylaw prohibiting members from performing online marriage ceremonies.

senses: Situated behind the eyes.
The province or area of an exarch.
ety: From exarch + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office, the concrete charge of it).

senses: The condition quality of being frail, physically, mentally, or morally; weakness of resolution; liability to be deceived.
A fault proceeding from weakness; foible; sin of infirmity.
ety: From Middle English frelete, frailte, from Old French fraileté, from Latin fragilitās. By surface analysis, frail + -ty. Doublet of fragility.

senses: To become a pupa.
examples: But first. Attend me, as I pupate!

senses: A cigar made with very dark tobacco.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish oscuro (“dark”). Doublet of obscure.

senses: Someone or something that farts.
A bed or sleeping bag
ety: From Middle English farter, fartare, fertere, equivalent to fart + -er (agent noun suffix), or, for a bed or sleeping bag, + -er (patient suffix). Cognate with German Furzer (“farter”).

senses: Computer science generally.
Likely to skid, or cause skidding.
Containing skidmarks.
A small armadillo (Zaedyus pichiy), native to Argentina, which is the only armadillo known to hibernate.
One of an order of priests among certain groups of Celts before the adoption of Abrahamic religions.
A priest or mage who uses magic based on nature or trees.
ety: Borrowed from French druide, from Old French, via Latin Druidae, from Gaulish *druwits, from Proto-Celtic *druwits (literally either “oak-knower” or “firm knower, great sage”), from either Proto-Indo-European *dóru (“tree”) or *drew- (“solid, firm, hard”) and *weyd- (“to see, to have knowledge”) (whence also English wizard; Proto-Slavic *vědьma (> Russian ве́дьма (védʹma))). The earliest record of the term in Latin is by Julius Caesar in the first century B.C. in his De Bello Gallico. The native Celtic word for "druid" is first attested in Latin texts as druides (plural) and other texts also e

senses: An improvement on the phonograph, using a floating stylus to cut grooves into a wax-coated cardboard cylinder.
An optical device for showing (or photographing) an image when projected upon the atmosphere as a screen.
examples: And then I see that the grip she was carrying was one of them little graphophones.

senses: A person who identifies with, or has loyalty to, a tribe or similar group.
An examination of esophagus, stomach and duodenum using endoscope.
A magistral line.
Powdered copper pyrites used in the amalgamation of ores of silver, as at the Spanish mines of Mexico and South America.
ety: Borrowed from Middle French magistral, from Latin magistrālis, from magister (“master, teacher”) + -ālis. Doublet of mistral.

senses: a person who anthologizes
A type of tutti-frutti or Neapolitan ice cream with nuts and candied fruits.
Synonym of cassata siciliana.
ety: Borrowed from Italian cassata (“cassata siciliana”), from Sicilian cassata, probably from Vulgar Latin *cāseāta, from cāseus (“cheese”). Compare Maltese qassata (“savoury pastry with ricotta filling”), confirming that the use of ricotta cheese is what unites all of the relevant dishes (and hence probably the original meaning).

senses: A rising swell.
ety: By surface analysis, up- + swell. Cognate with Dutch opzwellen, German aufschwellen.

senses: The lodging-house of a geisha.
examples: My advice to you is: work very hard, and never leave the okiya without permission.

senses: Dyed with henna.
examples: Her deeply hennaed hair, almost black at the roots, straggled loosely down both sides of her long face.
Lambert's hair is sometimes red, sometimes not, but nowadays it is hennaed and often pinned back with a mother-of-pearl comb.

senses: Someone who asks a question.
ety: From Middle English asker, axer, equivalent to ask + -er.

senses: A flat stone used to pave a pathway, such as a walkway to one's home.
One who paves; one who lays pavement.
A road paving machine, a machine to lay asphalt on roads.
A Muslim holy man.
In France (originally Provence), a small, hand-painted, terracotta figurine of a nativity character.
ety: Borrowed from French santon, from Spanish santón.
examples: Also we had brought a huge family of little santons of painted terracotta for the crêche.

senses: The short coarser fibers of flax or hemp; tow.
ety: From Middle English herdes, hurdes, plural of herde (“piece of hards”), from Old English heordan (“hards of flax, tow”), weak feminine plural of heorde (“headhair”), from Proto-West Germanic *heʀdā, from Proto-Germanic *hezdǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *kes- (“to comb, card”).

senses: A double-edged sword from India, used ceremonially in Sikhism.
A religious symbol of Sikhism, ⟨☬⟩, having the shape of three swords: a khanda, a chakram and two kirpans.
ety: Borrowed from Punjabi ਖੰਡਾ (khaṇḍā), from Sanskrit खड्ग (khaḍga).

senses: A person who manufactures glass.
Someone who plays a harp, especially a pedal harp.
Quite dry, relatively dry.
Turpentine or turpentine substitute.
The second coming of Christ.
examples: Only one wearing the masculine uniform can (provisionally, and till the Parousia) represent the Lord to the Church: for we are all, corporately and individually, feminine to Him.

senses: A type of circle dance originating in Catalonia.
examples: The Sardanas are danced in a circle. They are danced to the music of a curious orchestra of eleven instruments.

senses: A north-eastern English dish of deep-fried breaded chicken topped with béchamel sauce and cheese, sometimes served like a pizza with additional toppings.
ety: From parmesan + -o, from the original name of the dish, escalope parmesan.
examples: But I hadn't eaten since breakfast, and felt sure that a parmo's bark (smell and appearance) could not possibly be as bad as its bite (taste).

senses: A style of heavy overcoat, originally one with a short cloak on the shoulder; also, a style of frock coat with slanted pockets and velvet trimmings.
A type of corded tape used in dressmaking; a Petersham ribbon.
A thick woollen fabric used to make coats; Petersham cloth.
examples: She stopped at the landing window, tucking the frayed end of the petersham under the frame of the buckle…

senses: A cat-o'-nine-tails.
ety: From Middle English cattal, cattyle (also as cattestail), equivalent to cat + tail.

senses: Someone who dissembles.
ety: A modification of earlier dissimuler (from Middle English dissimulour) after resemble and semblance; equivalent to dissemble + -er.

senses: Someone who lives on a pension, especially the retirement or old age pension.
Someone who is at the age at which one typically receives a pension; an elderly person.
ety: From Middle English pensioner, from Anglo-Norman pensionner and Old French pensionnier, from Medieval Latin pēnsiōnārius. By surface analysis, pension + -er.

senses: Not rotating or not pertaining to rotation.
The doctrine that life involves some immaterial "vital force", and cannot be explained scientifically.
examples: It seems to me that in vitalism, there are people who are anti-Christian, like Bronze Age Pervert, like the Nazis.

senses: Peers as a group; the titled nobility or aristocracy.
The rank or title of a peer or peeress.
A book listing such people and their families.
ety: Inherited from Middle English perage, from Old French parage. By surface analysis, peer + -age. Doublet of parage.

senses: One who relates, or tells; a narrator.
One who relates, associates, or links things together.
